This extreme longevity is thought to buffer the population against intermittent recruitment failures by allowing repeated spawning opportunities across many decades. Comparative data from congeneric species such as Chasmistes cujus suggest that such extended lifespans are a conserved trait within the genus, likely linked to the oligotrophic, cold-water environments they inhabit.

This delayed puberty is ecologically significant because it increases the vulnerability of juveniles to predation and environmental stochasticity before they reach a size that confers reproductive competence.
